topStories.rawBody: GPT-6 models design protein structures and sequences using reasoning and code. Lab tests found evidence of binding across five targets.
topStories.bodyText: GPT-6 models demonstrate intrinsic protein-design capabilities | OpenAI OpenAI November 24, 2026 Our GPT‑6 family of models can design new protein shapes and the sequence of their chemical building blocks using only reasoning and code, without calling specialized biology models to generate those designs. An internal research model matched or outperformed specialized models on many protein design tasks. Researchers could also guide designs by prompting the model on where a protein should attach and what shape it should take. In lab tests with Onava, proteins based on GPT‑6.2’s designs showed evidence of binding, or attachment, across five targets. Redesigned antibodies also retained binding. Specialized models helped supply sequences and select candidates for testing. The models’ written reasoning and code suggest they draw on math, physics, chemistry, and biological knowledge to reason about protein shapes and interactions with other molecules. In a preprint titled GPT‑6 as a Universal Foundation Model for Protein Biology: Beyond Specialized Models , we show that our GPT‑6 family of models has intrinsic capabilities for designing new proteins: the models can design new protein structures and sequences without relying on specialized biology models, using only reasoning and general-purpose coding tools. Using and coordinating these specialized models requires substantial expertise. Each accepts particular kinds of inputs and constraints, and these models cannot easily accept new kinds of information without changes to their software or additional training. In contrast, a general-purpose model capable of performing the work of multiple specialized models can easily adapt to new instructions and requirements. Points farther from the center indicate better performance. Newer generations of models improved on many of the 14 protein tasks tested. The model’s written reasoning and code show it drawing on math, physics, chemistry and biology to design a protein intended to attach to IL-7Rα. It examines the target’s surface, arranges five coiled sections into a protein shape, and checks how the two proteins could fit together. Laboratory Experiment 1: Designing small proteins that bind to a target We gave GPT‑6.2 the three-dimensional structures of five target proteins and marked where we wanted a minibinder to attach. It then wrote code to create three-dimensional designs for potential minibinders, without using specialized protein AI models. To turn GPT‑6.2’s three-dimensional designs into proteins we could test in the lab, we needed amino acid sequences that would fold into the proposed structures. We used a specialized AI model called SolubleMPNN to suggest sequences for each design. Other specialized protein models helped us select candidates predicted to fold as designed and bind at the intended site on the target. GPT‑6.2 designed shapes for small proteins intended to attach to chosen targets. Specialized models then proposed amino acid sequences—the order of the proteins’ chemical building blocks—and helped select designs for our research partner Onava to make and test in the lab. An internal research model designed shapes for small proteins intended to attach to the target proteins shown in gray. The colored shapes compare each design with a computational prediction of how the protein would fold and fit against its target. Laboratory Experiment 2: Designing new sequences for 3D protein structures We tested whether GPT‑6.2 could design the sequences itself. We gave it three-dimensional models of how existing minibinders fit against their targets, withheld the original amino acid sequences, and asked it to propose new ones. Specialized models helped us choose which proteins to make and test in the lab.

topStories.bodyText: How iFood scales coding agents across 15,000 repositories | OpenAI OpenAI November 24, 2026 as many vulnerabilities fixed through the security platform The Remote Agents Platform turned engineering tasks into API calls: teams delegate the work, execution takes place in a remote sandbox, and the result comes back as a merge request. In the internal security platform, the number of vulnerabilities fixed more than doubled. iFood maintains more than 15,000 code repositories. Each periodically needs specific tasks performed: validating code to ensure it meets internal standards, fixing vulnerable dependencies, or running an analysis. None of these tasks is difficult on its own. The challenge comes when those tasks multiply. “Solving this for one repository is easy. The challenge is solving it at scale,” says Victor Coelho, Senior Software Engineer at iFood. “The Remote Agents Platform is designed to make it possible to solve this at scale across all 15,000 repositories.” Before the platform, each team tackled the problem in its own way—and they all ran into the same obstacle. “Before, we had fragmented solutions. Imagine several teams at iFood trying to solve different problems, but without this layer, this agentic runtime, available to them. In the end, those solutions always ran into the same problem.” What was missing wasn’t intelligence or a use case. It was execution infrastructure. A dedicated runtime . A coding agent in the cloud, accessible through an API The team describes the Remote Agents Platform as an API that launches a remote agentic coding task. The cycle has three steps: the user submits a prompt and environment requirements through a REST call; the platform processes the task on a dedicated remote runner inside an isolated sandbox; and the result is retrieved later. “The platform’s entry point, its interface, is a simple REST API. Users can use this API to create the runs they need. Internally, we handle and manage the entire lifecycle and delegate execution to isolated sandboxes,” he explains. Task progress can be monitored in real time. The runner’s internal design alternates between two different types of steps—and that combination makes the overall workflow predictable. Deterministic steps bookend the workflow: cloning the repository, importing the skills the agent can use, and setting up the working branch at the start; publishing the merge request and making the generated artifacts available at the end. In between is the agentic execution itself, running GPT‑5.6 Luna inside the sandbox. “It’s a combination of those two things: deterministic steps and agentic execution within the workflow.” The sandbox runs Ubuntu and includes the toolchains iFood’s ecosystem requires—Python, Java, Kotlin, C#, TypeScript, Rust, JavaScript, and Go—along with general-purpose tools. Beyond the sandbox, the agent can access Nexus, GitLab, Docker, Snyk, Kubernetes, and AWS.

topStories.rawBody: GPT 6.2 Astra Solves a Historical Mystery Here's an interesting case-study in using GPT-6.2 Astra for historical research, from history professor Mark Humphries: With only minimal prompting, GPT-6.2 Astra was able to autonomously identify the creator of an anonymous 1808 sketchbook held at Yale’s Beinecke Library . It did so extremely quickly (in just 22 minutes), using publicly available primary and secondary sources. To do so, it discovered a little known source in a paper archive, predicted that it would prove its hypothesis if examined and, in the end, it did. Not only that, but this new source turns out to be a major find on its own that will be of significant interest to both Canadian and fur trade historians. Here's the digitized sketchbook . Astra found a diary reference reference to a visit by the vicomte de Chabot dated five days before a date mentioned in the sketchbook at a nearby river, and suggested that Chabot's journal of his travels (only available by order from Cleveland State University) might confirm that the sketchbook was his work. Are historians due for a round of Deep Blue ? Mark thinks it will be mild: But if the experience of mathematics is any guide, we can also anticipate that sometime next spring or summer we’ll face a sort of crisis of confidence as we struggle to understand how to respond to agentic systems that can do things human historians cannot. To be fair, that crisis will almost certainly be less profound for us than it is for math. The problem in mathematics, of course, is that solving hard math problems was the whole game. Historians, on the other hand, constantly reinterpret the past in light of an evolving present; we don’t chase a single universal truth. We also (in the ideal at least) write books and articles that are closer to works of philosophy and literature than they are to scientific tracts. Humanity is thus something of a requirement for the production of historical literature. Tags: history , ai , generative-ai , llms , ai-assisted-search , deep-blue , gpt-6-astra

topStories.rawBody: Release: datasette-charts 0.2a0 I introduced this new charting plugin for Datasette yesterday . Today it's gained integration with Datasette Agent , so now you can ask chat for a chart and it will create one for you using the same underlying chart suggestion and generation tools. Here's a demo video, recorded on agent.datasette.io where you can sign in with GitHub to try the plugin yourself: Download the video (MP4) I prompt Datasette Agent to "Use #stats to show sqlite-utils downloads over time as a chart" - where typing "#stats" opens a table search box. It shows me a chart inline in the chat, and when I click "Open in the chart builder" it opens the chart in a panel along with the table page. I use the table page to switch to a chart of "datasette", then when I ask the agent "what does the chart show?" it notices that I changed the content in the panel and describes the new Datasette chart to me. Here's a Markdown export of the chat from the video. Tags: datasette-agent , datasette , visualization

items.rawBody: GPT-6 models design protein structures and sequences using reasoning and code. Lab tests found evidence of binding across five targets.
items.bodyText: GPT-6 models demonstrate intrinsic protein-design capabilities | OpenAI OpenAI November 24, 2026 Our GPT‑6 family of models can design new protein shapes and the sequence of their chemical building blocks using only reasoning and code, without calling specialized biology models to generate those designs. An internal research model matched or outperformed specialized models on many protein design tasks. Researchers could also guide designs by prompting the model on where a protein should attach and what shape it should take. In lab tests with Onava, proteins based on GPT‑6.2’s designs showed evidence of binding, or attachment, across five targets. Redesigned antibodies also retained binding. Specialized models helped supply sequences and select candidates for testing. The models’ written reasoning and code suggest they draw on math, physics, chemistry, and biological knowledge to reason about protein shapes and interactions with other molecules. In a preprint titled GPT‑6 as a Universal Foundation Model for Protein Biology: Beyond Specialized Models , we show that our GPT‑6 family of models has intrinsic capabilities for designing new proteins: the models can design new protein structures and sequences without relying on specialized biology models, using only reasoning and general-purpose coding tools. Using and coordinating these specialized models requires substantial expertise. Each accepts particular kinds of inputs and constraints, and these models cannot easily accept new kinds of information without changes to their software or additional training. In contrast, a general-purpose model capable of performing the work of multiple specialized models can easily adapt to new instructions and requirements. Points farther from the center indicate better performance. Newer generations of models improved on many of the 14 protein tasks tested. The model’s written reasoning and code show it drawing on math, physics, chemistry and biology to design a protein intended to attach to IL-7Rα. It examines the target’s surface, arranges five coiled sections into a protein shape, and checks how the two proteins could fit together. Laboratory Experiment 1: Designing small proteins that bind to a target We gave GPT‑6.2 the three-dimensional structures of five target proteins and marked where we wanted a minibinder to attach. It then wrote code to create three-dimensional designs for potential minibinders, without using specialized protein AI models. To turn GPT‑6.2’s three-dimensional designs into proteins we could test in the lab, we needed amino acid sequences that would fold into the proposed structures. We used a specialized AI model called SolubleMPNN to suggest sequences for each design. Other specialized protein models helped us select candidates predicted to fold as designed and bind at the intended site on the target. GPT‑6.2 designed shapes for small proteins intended to attach to chosen targets. Specialized models then proposed amino acid sequences—the order of the proteins’ chemical building blocks—and helped select designs for our research partner Onava to make and test in the lab. An internal research model designed shapes for small proteins intended to attach to the target proteins shown in gray. The colored shapes compare each design with a computational prediction of how the protein would fold and fit against its target. Laboratory Experiment 2: Designing new sequences for 3D protein structures We tested whether GPT‑6.2 could design the sequences itself. We gave it three-dimensional models of how existing minibinders fit against their targets, withheld the original amino acid sequences, and asked it to propose new ones. Specialized models helped us choose which proteins to make and test in the lab.

items.bodyText: How iFood scales coding agents across 15,000 repositories | OpenAI OpenAI November 24, 2026 as many vulnerabilities fixed through the security platform The Remote Agents Platform turned engineering tasks into API calls: teams delegate the work, execution takes place in a remote sandbox, and the result comes back as a merge request. In the internal security platform, the number of vulnerabilities fixed more than doubled. iFood maintains more than 15,000 code repositories. Each periodically needs specific tasks performed: validating code to ensure it meets internal standards, fixing vulnerable dependencies, or running an analysis. None of these tasks is difficult on its own. The challenge comes when those tasks multiply. “Solving this for one repository is easy. The challenge is solving it at scale,” says Victor Coelho, Senior Software Engineer at iFood. “The Remote Agents Platform is designed to make it possible to solve this at scale across all 15,000 repositories.” Before the platform, each team tackled the problem in its own way—and they all ran into the same obstacle. “Before, we had fragmented solutions. Imagine several teams at iFood trying to solve different problems, but without this layer, this agentic runtime, available to them. In the end, those solutions always ran into the same problem.” What was missing wasn’t intelligence or a use case. It was execution infrastructure. A dedicated runtime . A coding agent in the cloud, accessible through an API The team describes the Remote Agents Platform as an API that launches a remote agentic coding task. The cycle has three steps: the user submits a prompt and environment requirements through a REST call; the platform processes the task on a dedicated remote runner inside an isolated sandbox; and the result is retrieved later. “The platform’s entry point, its interface, is a simple REST API. Users can use this API to create the runs they need. Internally, we handle and manage the entire lifecycle and delegate execution to isolated sandboxes,” he explains. Task progress can be monitored in real time. The runner’s internal design alternates between two different types of steps—and that combination makes the overall workflow predictable. Deterministic steps bookend the workflow: cloning the repository, importing the skills the agent can use, and setting up the working branch at the start; publishing the merge request and making the generated artifacts available at the end. In between is the agentic execution itself, running GPT‑5.6 Luna inside the sandbox. “It’s a combination of those two things: deterministic steps and agentic execution within the workflow.” The sandbox runs Ubuntu and includes the toolchains iFood’s ecosystem requires—Python, Java, Kotlin, C#, TypeScript, Rust, JavaScript, and Go—along with general-purpose tools. Beyond the sandbox, the agent can access Nexus, GitLab, Docker, Snyk, Kubernetes, and AWS.

items.rawBody: GPT 6.2 Astra Solves a Historical Mystery Here's an interesting case-study in using GPT-6.2 Astra for historical research, from history professor Mark Humphries: With only minimal prompting, GPT-6.2 Astra was able to autonomously identify the creator of an anonymous 1808 sketchbook held at Yale’s Beinecke Library . It did so extremely quickly (in just 22 minutes), using publicly available primary and secondary sources. To do so, it discovered a little known source in a paper archive, predicted that it would prove its hypothesis if examined and, in the end, it did. Not only that, but this new source turns out to be a major find on its own that will be of significant interest to both Canadian and fur trade historians. Here's the digitized sketchbook . Astra found a diary reference reference to a visit by the vicomte de Chabot dated five days before a date mentioned in the sketchbook at a nearby river, and suggested that Chabot's journal of his travels (only available by order from Cleveland State University) might confirm that the sketchbook was his work. Are historians due for a round of Deep Blue ? Mark thinks it will be mild: But if the experience of mathematics is any guide, we can also anticipate that sometime next spring or summer we’ll face a sort of crisis of confidence as we struggle to understand how to respond to agentic systems that can do things human historians cannot. To be fair, that crisis will almost certainly be less profound for us than it is for math. The problem in mathematics, of course, is that solving hard math problems was the whole game. Historians, on the other hand, constantly reinterpret the past in light of an evolving present; we don’t chase a single universal truth. We also (in the ideal at least) write books and articles that are closer to works of philosophy and literature than they are to scientific tracts. Humanity is thus something of a requirement for the production of historical literature. Tags: history , ai , generative-ai , llms , ai-assisted-search , deep-blue , gpt-6-astra

items.rawBody: Release: datasette-charts 0.2a0 I introduced this new charting plugin for Datasette yesterday . Today it's gained integration with Datasette Agent , so now you can ask chat for a chart and it will create one for you using the same underlying chart suggestion and generation tools. Here's a demo video, recorded on agent.datasette.io where you can sign in with GitHub to try the plugin yourself: Download the video (MP4) I prompt Datasette Agent to "Use #stats to show sqlite-utils downloads over time as a chart" - where typing "#stats" opens a table search box. It shows me a chart inline in the chat, and when I click "Open in the chart builder" it opens the chart in a panel along with the table page. items.rawBody: GLM-5.4: Toward Generalized Coding with Our First Loop Transformer GLM 5.4 is now available from Chinese AI lab Z.ai. It's their first model to use a looped transformer architecture, which they describe like this: In a standard Transformer, each layer runs once per forward pass. In a Loop Transformer, a group of weight-shared layers runs for multiple iterations, refining the hidden states from the previous pass. This gives us a deeper network without increasing the parameter count. This is the second mention of looped transformers I've seen in the past week - the first was Inkling 2 Mini from Thinking Machines Lab on November 20th, who said: Inkling 2 Mini is a looped transformer, running the middle layers of the model three times for every token. This allows the model to apply more reasoning and reach the right answer with fewer tokens, especially on tasks such as agentic coding that depend on reasoning quality. GLM 5.4 is not yet available as open weights: We plan to open-source the model weights responsibly after completing necessary safety hardening. I tried it out using the Z.ai API, for which I had to sign up for their Coding Plan subscription because 5.4 cannot currently be accessed through the regular API. It turns out both coding plan and regular API share the same OpenAI-compatible Responses API (at https://api.z.ai/api/v1 ), and the API key for the coding plan worked with that and gave me access to the new model. I built a llm-glm plugin , then realized that llm-zai by Tommy Hughes already exists! I've shipped mine purely because llm-zai doesn't yet support the new model, but I'll likely retire mine once that plugin catches up. Here are pelicans for GLM-5.4 on low, high, and max. This is the max one: I realized I never ran pelicans for GLM-5.3, so here those are for the same effort levels. They look similar in quality to 5.4. It's interesting how GLM 5.1 and GLM 5.2 produced radically different pelicans from other models. The pelicans for 5.3 and 5.4 are much more comparable to those I get from OpenAI or Anthropic models - the previous generations had their own distinctive look. I made a comparison grid showing the four generations of GLM pelicans all in one place. The style transition between 5.2 and 5.3 is pretty stark. Tags: ai , generative-ai , llms , llm , pelican-riding-a-bicycle , llm-release , ai-in-china , glm

items.rawBody: Ladybird is an astonishingly ambitious project: a new browser, in 2026, with its own implementation of most of the key components - HTML parsing, CSS engine, layout, JavaScript, even WebAssembly. It still uses a few external components - things like HarfBuzz for text shaping, Skia for 2D graphics, ffmpeg for video, and SQLite for the things you do with SQLite. Everything else is part of Ladybird, or code brought in from Ladybird's even more ambitious predecessor project SerenityOS . This morning the Ladybird project released their first alpha , which means you can now install the browser (on macOS or Linux) without having to compile it yourself! I've been trying it out today, and it's very impressive. It feels fast, the UI is lightweight and intuitive, and most of the websites I've tried to load in it have worked as they should. It looks like this (showing my video-compressor tool): Here's the process tree after I opened six tabs in one window and another tab in a second window (generated by this script , thanks Claude): Ladybird (72925) [240 MB] └── Hub (72926) [61 MB] ├── RequestServer (72927) [29 MB] ├── ProcessReaper (72928) [1 MB] ├── Compositor (72930) [123 MB] ├── RequestServer (72953) [36 MB] ├── WebContent (72984) [819 MB] ├── MediaServer (73006) [118 MB] ├── VideoDecoderServer (73007) [20 MB] ├── WebContent (73052) [144 MB] ├── WebContent (73057) [73 MB] ├── WebContent (73073) [166 MB] ├── WebContent (73094) [70 MB] ├── WebContent (73112) [116 MB] ├── RequestServer (73113) [27 MB] └── WebContent (73185) [60 MB] Ladybird runs different tabs in different processes, an isolation mechanism used by most browsers (well, technically Chrome uses a process-per-site). I tried Ladybird against several of my more advanced tool examples - like the video-compressor shown above, which runs ffmpeg compiled to WebAssembly. I had it resize its own screenshot using my image-resize tool . It happily runs my Pyodide REPL (Python compiled to WebAssembly) too. The one thing I tried that didn't work was Datasette Lite , which runs Pyodide in a complicated arrangement of service workers and web workers. Attempting to start Datasette Lite displays this error: undefined is not a function (evaluated from 'navigator.serviceWorker.startMessages') I filed an issue about this , then found a FIXME annotation in the source code. The October explosion The project has been leaning heavily into coding agents this year. On February 23, 2026 Andreas Kling published Ladybird adopts Rust, with help from AI , describing how they ported parts of their LibJS JavaScript engine from C++ to 25,000 lines of Rust in two weeks using Claude Code and Codex. Here's the GitHub contributions chart for Ladybird over the past twelve months: That uptick in October corresponds to the landing of a wealth of big improvements. This Month in Ladybird — October 2026 describes what happened. In addition to moving style and layout to their own thread, landing a new JavaScript JIT, and replacing their C++ with Cranelift WebAssembly engine with new code that achieved a 7x boost on the JetStream 3 WASM benchmark , they gained 75,650 new passes on the ~2.25 million subtest web-platform-tests suite, beating Safari! How did they do that? Coding agents: Most of that gain came in five days, from about 2.12 million on October 22 to about 2.18 million on October 27. We pointed AI coding agents at WPT and asked them to fill in missing functionality. They made lots of small fixes, and those added up. Our biggest gains for the month were about 30,000 in /css and 10,000 in /editing . I'm interested in what models they are using here - I know Andreas uses Codex and Claude Code, but I haven't seen him talk about specific model versions. Claude Opus 5.5 came out on September 22, 2026 and Claude Fable 5.2 on November 9, 2026 (after that window). I'd love to know what they were using for that huge leap in the last week of October. Should you use Ladybird? Here's what Andreas says about Ladybird's suitability for use as a daily browser: This is an alpha, so some websites won’t work, and it will crash sometimes. When that happens, tell us! You can report a broken site from inside the browser. After a crash, you can read the crash report and decide whether to send it. Our privacy policy has the details. We want security nerds to hack it! A new browser gets hacked, over and over, and that’s part of the process, so we make no promises about security today. When you pwn us, please tell us how so we can harden Ladybird! Given how hard it is to secure a web browser, and the hostility of the environment they operate in, I won't be using Ladybird to sign into GitHub or Gmail or any of my other sensitive accounts. I'm going to keep it around for anonymous browsing though, partly to participate in the testing efforts but mainly because it gives me a glimmer of optimism to see a promising new entrant in the stagnant browser engine market start to grow its wings. Tags: browsers , open-source , ai , rust , webassembly , generative-ai , llms , andreas-kling , ladybird , coding-agents

items.rawBody: Release: datasette-charts 0.1a0 I've been thinking about this problem for over a year now, but on Sunday I finally fired up Claude Fable 5.2 to build an initial prototype. The prototype went so well that this is now a full plugin. You can try it out in Datasette Lite here . It looks like this: The new charts plugin works against any table or arbitrary SQL query in Datasette. It defines several different chart types (using vendored D3 , Observable Plot , and topojson-client ), each with a set of heuristics for identifying when they might be a good match for a specific set of rows. Those suggestion thumbnails at the top are actual visualizations driven by the data, and selecting one pulls up the full chart along with tools for modifying it. You can also manually construct a chart from scratch. As with other Datasette visualization plugins, the current state of your chart is persisted in a #fragment in the URL - so you can bookmark charts or share them with others. The most important feature is that the charts take all rows into account . Previous charting plugins like datasette-vega would only show charts for the current page of results, generally up to 100 rows. The new plugin compiles each chart to a SQL query that aggregates across the entire result set (potentially millions of rows) using GROUP BY, time bucketing, and window functions. Each query returns a result capped at 5,000 rows, suitable for display on the chart. The plugin uses sampling to help suggest charts for larger tables without evaluating the full result set. I'm really happy with this initial release of the plugin. It's still very much an alpha, but it's the closest I've got to the dream of Datasette helping visualize data with as little required direction from the user as possible. items.rawBody: Token fraud is here and it’s BAD (YouTube) Claire Vo runs ChatPRD , an AI platform that helps product managers "turn an idea into a spec". The product has been live since the GPT-4 era, and Claire has been building it in public for much of that time. In this YouTube video (see also the accompanying Twitter post ) Claire describes the flood of token fraud she has seen from groups abusing the product's free trial, sometimes just to get free AI usage but often to resell tokens or run other commercial enterprises on top of the ChatPRD agent. I am funding a international Roblox and Fortnite map studio. They run a loop of free trials and promo codes and then tunnel to my agent and use it to build Roblox and Fortnite maps. Apparently one of the common prompts Claire saw running through her agent involved SVGs of pelicans riding bicycles! Presumably the token scammers are using that to help sniff the underlying models - different model families have a definite signature, and I've used it like this in the past to try and guess the identity of stealth preview models on platforms like OpenRouter. Claire is winding down her free trials entirely, which sadly looks like the right decision in the face of this abuse. Tags: youtube , ai , generative-ai , llms , pelican-riding-a-bicycle , ai-misuse

items.rawBody: Release: llm-gemini 0.38 Today Google introduced Gemini 4 Neon . I wrote recently about how confusing the pricing for the Gemini 4 series was - Neon has somehow made this even worse. Previously the Gemini 4 lineup was Hydrogen, Argon, and Carbon - where Argon and Carbon were the same price , and Hydrogen was 3/4 of that price now but will be 1/4 of that price when the other two double an 1st December once their initial discount pricing expires. The Neon announcement pretends that Argon doesn't exist. Here's their new image explaining the model line-up: So the lineup now, from most to least expensive, is Carbon, Neon, Hydrogen. Except Carbon is currently half price, so right now Neon ($3/million input, $15/million output) is the most expensive of the three - then Carbon ($2/$10), then Hydrogen ($1.50/$7.50). I guess this will make more sense when Carbon doubles to $4/$20 on December 1st. I ran some pelicans through the three reasoning levels for Neon - low, medium, high. I dropped Argon from my Gemini 4 comparison grid - here's the new Gemini 4 lineup, where the Neon pelicans do look better than Hydrogen and worse than Carbon: As I've done with several recent models , I also fired the following prompt against Gemini 4 Neon on "extra" effort level in Google Antigravity: Make a three js animation where yonkers stands up as a big mech (cool stand up motion) and stomps around manhattan and queens and Brooklyn, use openstreetmap mapping data Here's the result . items.rawBody: Release: datasette-arrows 0.1a0 Datasette 1.0a43 added the ability for plugins to implement streaming export formats. Datasette core supports streaming CSV and TSV - you can export millions of lines of data from a table without needing to load it all into memory, because those two file formats support streaming data in chunks. The register_output_renderer() plugin hook can now be used to implement the same pattern for other formats. I've learned never to release a new plugin feature without accompanying it with a plugin that uses it. Claude Fable 5.2 suggested the Apache Arrow streaming format as a good option, and built this plugin in almost a single shot. Add the plugin to Datasette ( datasette install datasette-arrows ) and the export dialog gains this new Arrow option: This screenshot is from Datasette's main branch - the most recent release doesn't yet group streaming formats such as Arrow with the TSV and CSV in the "All rows in this table" section, but that's coming in the next alpha release. Tags: datasette , projects

items.rawBody: External sandboxes for coding agents I've been exploring new ways to sandbox code that is executed by agents, with a focus on making it safer to try out local models without worrying that a mistake or prompt injection attack might cause them to take damaging actions on a machine. I worked on this project with Prime Radiant , the AI research lab behind Superpowers and other projects . My post on the Prime Radiant blog introduces the external sandbox pattern, where code executed by the agent runs inside a dedicated sandbox while the agent itself lives outside of that sandbox. To demonstrate this pattern we've released three sandbox server implementations: external-sandbox-v86 runs a Node.js server which then uses v86 to run Alpine Linux inside WebAssembly. external-sandbox-container is a Python web server which runs the sandbox in Alpine Linux inside an Apple Containers instance. external-sandbox-quicksand is another Python web server, this time using Microsoft's Quicksand sandboxing library, which bundles QEMU and Alpine Linux in a Python package! Each of these implementations offers the same localhost API. You can then configure Pi, Claude Code, or Codex to send API calls to that sandbox any time they want to execute code. The sandboxes also include an optional HTTP/HTTPS allow-list proxy, so you can control exactly which hosts your agent's code is allowed to communicate with - plus a credential replacement mechanism to make authenticated API calls without sharing a secret with the agent. Here's the UI you can use to reconfigure that proxy while the sandbox is still running: I continue to be fascinated by the challenge of safely running untrusted code. This external sandbox pattern provides a neat way to experiment with different approaches. Tags: sandboxing , security , ai , webassembly , generative-ai , llms , coding-agents , claude-code , codex , pi

items.rawBody: GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol OpenAI: We’re introducing GPT‑6.2 Astra, our new frontier model for your hardest projects, and GPT‑6.2 Sol, our efficient, versatile model for everyday work. They're available in the API as gpt-6.2-astra and gpt-6.2-sol . I shipped LLM 0.38 with support for the new models. 6.2 Astra is 80% of the price of 6 Astra - $8/MTok input and $40/MTok output, the same price as Claude Fable 5.2 (which was also 80% of its predecessor). 6 Astra and Fable 5 were both $10/$50. The cached price is an even bigger discount - $0.40/million compared to $1/million for the older model. This is great news for longer running agentic sessions. GPT-6.2 Sol is the same $2/$10 price as 6.1 Sol and 6 Sol - which are half the price of GPT-5.6 Sol ($4/$20). Here are the pelicans for GPT-6.2 Sol and for GPT-6.2 Astra . The 6.2 Astra max pelican looks like this: I have a full comparison grid here , but here's how the high/xhigh/max pelicans compare with the previous Sol and Astra releases: I also ran my most recent benchmark prompt against the two models, using "Ultra' effort levels in the Codex CLI: Make a three js animation where yonkers stands up as a big mech (cool stand up motion) and stomps around manhattan and queens and Brooklyn, use openstreetmap mapping data Here's Sol and here's Astra . Neither of them did a good enough job of morphing Yonkers into a big mech, at least in comparison to Claude Fable 5.2 and Gemini 4 Carbon . This video showing the Astra and Sol animations playing out at the same time: I created that video using GPT-6.2 Astra (Ultra) in the Codex desktop app by prompting: https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2026/yonkers-gpt-6.2-astra-ultra/index.html and https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2026/yonkers-gpt-6.2-sol-ultra/index.html are two videos of the same thing by two different models I need a video of the first 10 seconds where the top half of the video plays the first and the bottom half plays the second I need an overlaid label of "GPT-6.2 Astra" on the top half and "GPT-6.2 Sol" on the bottom half. These labels should be tastefully positioned. Make the video square and 2000x2000 pixels Then later: OK make it 20s Here's the exported transcript . The buzz around these new models is mixed at the moment. Astra 6.2 isn't scoring quite as high as Fable 5.2 on various benchmarks, and I've seen a few complaints that its communication style can be confusing. Theo Browne's review (in the form of a feedback letter he sent OpenAI during pre-release) has this useful example: When this model is working on long tasks, it can pull in a lot of subagents and manage them pretty well. It will then proceed to randomly ask you some weird internal implementation detail bullshit that you could not under any earthly circumstance understand, much less have input on . I sent "/goal make a new level for Outer Wilds". 2 hours in, it's "blocked" because it wanted to ask me "does r24's reviewer write it's clips to 24_g521.mp4 or 24_p11.mp4?" Tags: ai , openai , generative-ai , llms , llm-pricing , pelican-riding-a-bicycle , llm-release , theo-browne , gpt , yonkers-rising

items.rawBody: Datasette Lite is my port of the Datasette Python application to run directly in the browser using WebAssembly and Pyodide . I've released a complete rewrite of Datasette Lite using service workers, and it's now almost indistinguishable from the real server-side application. You can now do all of the following, using a carefully crafted URL to lite.datasette.io : Load client-side Datasette to browse any SQLite database, JSON file, CSV file or SQL script Select a released version of Datasette to load from PyPI Load a specific commit, tag, or branch name from the Datasette GitHub repository Pick from over 100 versions of SQLite to use with Datasette Install additional Datasette plugins from PyPI or URLs to wheel files, including JavaScript visualization tools The ability to load specific Datasette references, plugins, and SQLite versions makes this a fantastic tool for linking to demos of work-in-progress features or bug reproductions, without needing to spin up a full web server to serve that demo. As an example, consider the following URL: https://lite.datasette.io/?install=datasette-maplibre&url=https://gist.githubusercontent.com/simonw/39fa5d399465766039549912e2b3d291/raw/f6dfba99a75cbb8b5d9386223220eb52272767ee/demo.db&metadata=https://gist.githubusercontent.com/simonw/39fa5d399465766039549912e2b3d291/raw/f6dfba99a75cbb8b5d9386223220eb52272767ee/metadata.yml#/demo/capitals_and_countries%23map=0/4.2/180&color=continent Follow that link and, after a short loading screen, you'll find yourself on a page that looks like this: That's Datasette running the new datasette-maplibre plugin, loading up a database of GeoJSON shapes of countries and displaying both a combined map and individual boundary maps in a table. Let's break down that URL to see what it's doing: https://lite.datasette.io/ ?install=datasette-maplibre &url=https://.../demo.db &metadata=https://.../metadata.yml #/demo/capitals_and_countries%23map=0/4.2/180&color=continent The ?install=datasette-maplibre installs that additional plugin from PyPI. You can pass &install=... as many times as you like to load more plugins. &url=https://.../demo.db loads that SQLite database from the provided URL. These URLs need to have open CORS headers - I host files like this in Gists , because they provide an easy way to get open CORS headers on a web-hosted file. &metadata=https://.../metadata.yml loads this metadata.yml file . The metadata file adds HTML descriptions to various tables, and to the Datasette homepage. Visit that homepage here for a guided tour of the other features of that plugin, all defined in the metadata file. #/demo/capitals_and_countries%23map=0/4.2/180&color=continent is a fragment hash that turns into a location within Datasette - here it's loading the /demo/capitals_and_countries SQL view, then appending another fragment hash to it ( %23 is a URL-encoded # ) which tells the map plugin to zoom to a certain location and to set the color of the shapes on the map based on the continent column in the data. That URL is doing a lot of work! I wrote more about this trick for building URL-addressable software in URL-addressable Pyodide Python environments last year. The full set of supported URL arguments is described in the Datasette Lite README . I've already started using Datasette Lite as part of the Datasette development process. Here's a recent issue describing a pagination bug - I posted a comment there demonstrating the old, broken behavior and the new fix using links to Datasette Lite: Demo of the bug: https://lite.datasette.io/?ref=1.0a42&sql=https://gist.github.com/simonw/75ececf61d50e6e8d50f0c150150ee81#/data/scores?_size=2&_sort=score - click next and the second page is empty. Here's that same page with the bug fixed (running on 1.0a43): https://lite.datasette.io/?ref=1.0a43&sql=https://gist.github.com/simonw/75ececf61d50e6e8d50f0c150150ee81#/data/scores?_size=2&_sort=score How this works, using service workers Datasette Lite is not a new project. I launched the first version back in 2022 , originally as a bit of a joke (running server-side apps in the browser is pretty funny) but one that quickly started proving its value. The problem with that initial version is that it was a hack . It worked by running Datasette in a Pyodide web worker, simulating requests through that stack, then injecting the resulting HTML back into the top level page using innerHTML . This worked for basic Datasette, but meant that any feature that used JavaScript failed to work, because script tags in innerHTML don't execute, and the web worker tricks it used failed to load additional JavaScript or CSS files. The new version takes a completely different approach based on Service Workers . These allow JavaScript to intercept HTTP requests for new pages and resources and serve them from client-side code instead. Datasette Lite registers a service worker for the entire lite.datasette.io domain. The parent page then creates an iframe that sends requests for Datasette pages to URLs that look like this: /app/aa94e6851595/ # the homepage (HTML) /app/aa94e6851595/data/places # a table page (HTML) /app/aa94e6851595/-/static/navigation-search.js # (JavaScript) /app/a

items.rawBody: Release: datasette-maplibre 0.1a0 The first new Datasette geospatial plugin in quite a while! This one combines the excellent MapLibre GL library with OpenFreeMap , the free vector map server operated by Zsolt Ero (you should sponsor Zsolt on GitHub .) I built most of this with a single prompt to Claude Fable 5.2: Look at datasette-cluster-map and datasette-leaflet-geojson plugins, then look at ~/dev/tools/openfreemap-demo.html - then build a brand new Datasette plugin that uses maplibreGL and openfreemap and combines the features of those other two plugins - but be creative and think outside the box for other useful features the plugin might have "Be creative and think outside the box" resulted in a few neat ideas - my favorite is that it displays SVG previews of GeoJSON shapes, then loads a WebGL preview only when they scroll into view. I also had Claude build a comprehensive demo which works in the latest Datasette Lite, so you can visit this link to load the plugin and a demo database in your browser via Pyodide and WebAssembly. items.rawBody: Release: datasette-llm 0.1a11 datasette-llm is the intermediate plugin for Datasette that supports configuring LLMs for use with other Datasette plugins. This release adds support for OpenAI-compatible endpoints, so you can configure Datasette to use an LLM hosted anywhere that talks the OpenAI pseudo-standard web protocol. This means that if you're running local models with LM Studio or Ollama or llama.cpp (which just hit v1.0.0 ) you can run Datasette via uvx like this: wget https://datasette.io/content.db uvx --with datasette-agent datasette \ --root --secret 1 \ -s plugins.datasette-llm.default_model ' { "model": "lmstudio-qwen", "model_name": "qwen/qwen3.8-27b", "api_base": "http://localhost:1234/v1" } ' content.db And you'll get a local server running a Datasette Agent instance powered by your local model! Tags: uv , datasette-agent , llm , datasette , llms , ai , generative-ai

items.rawBody: Release: llm 0.37.3 A bug fix release for LLM , mainly to cover a problem with the most recent Homebrew package of the software. Homebrew now ships the latest SQLite, 3.54.1 , which includes a fix that broke LLM's logging code . Short version: in SQLite 3.54.0 the following SQL: select json_object('a', (select json_array(1))) Returns this: {"a":[1]} But in 3.54.1 the same query returns this: {"a":"[1]"} According to D. Richard Hipp : That was a bug fix. Per the documentation, (SELECT json_array(...)) returns SQL text, not JSON. Hence the 3.54.1 behavior is correct and 3.54.0 was a bug. The workaround looks like this: select json_object('a', json((select json_array(1)))) Tags: llm , webassembly , sqlite , generative-ai , ai , llms , d-richard-hipp

items.rawBody: Release: datasette 1.0a43 I've been leaning hard into Claude Fable 5.2 to help knock things off the 1.0 milestone , which is now 53% complete. The biggest 1.0 item in this release is streaming support for output renderers - the built-in TSV and CSV export mechanisms now use this as well, and plugins can register themselves as capable of streaming every row in a table in one go via the new Response.stream() method. There are a couple of security fixes, one of which I deemed deserving of a GitHub advisory : private stored queries could be exposed, granting access to the title and SQL of the query (but not allowing that query to be executed). There are dozens of smaller improvements. The row page JSON representation finally has a design suitable for 1.0 . A new <datasette-copy-button> Web Component provides copy-schema in various places. JSON in columns on the row page can be pretty-printed. There's a new DatasetteModal.confirm() JavaScript utility method. Plus dozens of bug fixes, including contributions by Zihan Dai , Peter Olkhovets , Ilya Khalafi , and Ankita Advitot . The feature I'm most excited about is a pretty tiny one: I've added CSS multi-page view transitions to Datasette! Here's the commit - key CSS is as follows: /* Enable cross-document view transitions, for anyone without prefers-reduced-motion */ @media ( prefers-reduced-motion : no-preference ) { @view-transition { navigation : auto ; } } /* .facet-results should morph from old position to new */ html : active-view-transition . content > . facet-results { view-transition-name : facet-results ; } /* So should a .table-wrapper, provided it contains .rows-and-columns */ html : active-view-transition . table-wrapper : has ( > table . rows-and-columns ) { view-transition-name : rows-table ; } With that in place, navigations within Datasette - still staunchly a multi-page application - feel more like an SPA. This works on Safari and Chrome at the moment and I believe supports for Firefox is due to land in Firefox 162 on December 8th 2026 (seeing as they are no longer feature-flagged in Firefox Nightly.) items.rawBody: The concept of recursive self-improvement (RSI) dates back to I. J. Good (1965) , where he defined an “ultraintelligent machine” as a system that can surpass humans in all intellectual activities and design better machines to improve itself. Yudkowsky (2008) used the phrase “recursive self-improvement” for a specific feedback loop: an AI uses its current intelligence to improve the cognitive machinery that produces its intelligence. This feedback loop in modern AI may indicate the model rewriting its own weights directly, or more broadly the model improves the training pipeline and the deployment system , which in turn enables a better successor model with improved performance across economically valuable tasks. The speed of research development in AI has been shown to drastically accelerated in frontier labs ( Anthropic ; OpenAI ).

items.rawBody: Scaling laws are one of the most critical empirical findings in deep learning. The observation is simple in form: the training loss $L$ decreases predictably as we scale up model size $N$, dataset size $D$, and compute $C$, following a power-law curve, which appears as a straight line on a log-log plot. We can view scaling laws as a framework for describing the relationship between compute, loss, model size and data; at its core, it is about how to allocate precious compute optimally between $N$ and $D$.

archiveItems.rawBody: PostgreSQL 19 Released Most years PostgreSQL ships a new release in September, but this year's release came two months later thanks mainly to the flurry of issues that the PostgreSQL team needed to address as part of the ongoing AI-reported vulnerability apocalypse. This release was definitely worth the wait. My favorite new feature is this one: For applications that send reads to standbys, PostgreSQL 19 adds "read-your-writes" consistency with the new WAIT FOR LSN command. A session on a standby can use WAIT FOR LSN to wait until the standby has replayed the write-ahead log (WAL) up to a specific log sequence number (LSN) before running a query, so the application can read data it just wrote on the primary. In practice, that looks like this: UPDATE movie SET genre = 'Dramatic' WHERE genre = 'Drama'; SELECT pg_current_wal_insert_lsn(); That returns a value like 0/0306EE20 . Store that somewhere (a signed cookie would work) such that on a subsequent request your application can do: WAIT FOR LSN '0/0306EE20' WITH (TIMEOUT '0.1s'); SELECT * FROM movie WHERE genre = 'Drama'; The timeout is optional - if you provide one you'll get an error if the replica you are talking to doesn't catch up within the specified time. I first encountered this pattern in Wikipedia , which has a hand-rolled version of this built against MySQL replication: In addition to this, MediaWiki attempts to ensure that the user sees events occurring on the wiki in chronological order. A few seconds of lag can be tolerated, as long as the user sees a consistent picture from subsequent requests. This is done by saving the primary binlog position in the session, and then at the start of each request, waiting for the replica to catch up to that position before doing any reads from it. Here's the relevant MediaWiki code , which these days uses MySQL's WAIT_FOR_EXECUTED_GTID_SET() function and falls back to SOURCE_POS_WAIT() . Via Lobste.rs Tags: mysql , postgresql , replication , scaling , wikipedia , ai-security-research
